papers.version_note: arXiv:2208.11510v4 (25 Nov 2022); AAAI-style main text followed by Supplementary Materials. The text layer carries the paper once. Greek letters that carry a subscript or a hat (epsilon_t and similar) were lost in the layer, so Theorem 1 prints its two constants as bare 't'. Figures 1 to 7 and the supplementary figures are images; their captions and the text around them were read.
papers.what_it_is: A proposal of quantum meta multi-agent reinforcement learning (QM2ARL) that trains a QNN's angle parameters as a meta Q-network, then its two-parameter measurement poles for local tasks, with an angle-to-pole noise regularizer, a convergence bound (Theorem 1), a pole memory, and classical-simulation experiments on a two-step game and a single-hop offloading task.

existing.note: The text layer holds Theorem 1's full statement (the stored note says it is cut before its bound). The bound is sin(alpha)/alpha times a sum of two constants indexed by t, on the expected angle training error with the regularization. Assumption 2 (bi-Lipschitz continuity of the meta Q-network) is also quoted; the stored value names only the second assumption by its content.
existing.value: The paper states Theorem 1: with Assumptions 1 and 2, the angle training error of a meta Q-network with angle-to-pole regularization at epoch t is upper bounded by a constant, the expectation of the error is at most sin α α times the sum of two constants indexed by t. Assumption 1 is the convergence of angle training without the regularization (error at most a constant for t ≥ 0) and Assumption 2 is that the meta Q-network is bi-Lipschitz continuous.

existing.certainty_reason: The statement and both assumptions are quoted from the main text; the proof is in the supplement (Lemmas 1 to 3 and 'Proof of Theorem 1').
existing.reader_inference: The bound is conditional on Assumption 1, which assumes the unregularized training already converges, so it shows the noise factor sin(alpha)/alpha scales the bound; it does not show that training converges. The supplementary proof is short: Lemma 2 and the final chain use an inequality for the noisy gradient, and equation (5) replaces the average of two parameter-shifted observables by the unshifted observable (an approximation the text marks with the 'approximately equal' sign). The final step states that one term is 'bounded to' the Assumption 1 constant and the other 'bound to constant' without computing the second constant. A reviewer should check the proof before the grade is set. The bound's sin(alpha)/alpha factor is below 1 for alpha above 0, so the bound shrinks as the noise grows, which sits oddly beside the experiments where larger alpha slows meta training (Fig. 5).

existing.note: The Concluding Remarks sentence is as stored, but the body places the slowdown in the meta-QNN angle-training stage and reports the opposite (faster convergence) for the local-QNN pole-training stage. All of it is measured on the two-step game. The body gives no direct test of generalization (no held-out environment); the conclusion's word 'generalizing' rests on the Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 observations.
existing.value: The authors report, on the two-step game, that a larger angle noise bound makes the meta-QNN angle training slower (the training loss grows with the noise and the meta Q-network ends farther from the optimal action-value), while the local-QNN pole training converges faster; the Concluding Remarks state that the angle-to-pole regularization is effective in generalizing the meta-QNN training, yet at the cost of compromising convergence speed.
existing.anchor: Impact of Angle-to-Pole Regularization (Fig. 5), Concluding Remarks
quotes: As shown in Fig. 5(a), the training loss is proportioned to the intensity of angle noise.
As shown in Fig. 5(c), the smaller angle bound, QM2ARL converges slowly, and when the angle bound is large, it shows faster convergence.
In summary, despite the angle noise regularizer making meta-QNN angle training slow convergence, the angle noise regularizer makes the local-QNN pole training fast convergence.
The results also showed that the proposed angle-to-pole regularization is effective in generalizing the meta-QNN training, yet at the cost of compromising convergence speed.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, read from figures, with no repeats or error bars stated.
existing.reader_inference: The slowdown named in the conclusion is the meta stage; the pole stage gets faster. The conclusion does not say which stage its 'convergence speed' cost applies to. No experiment measures generalization to an unseen environment; the evidence for 'generalizing' is the spread of action values over pole positions in Fig. 4 and the pole-memory runs.

existing.note: The Concluding Remarks sentence is as stored. The body discusses the comparison only in the single-hop offloading environment (Fig. 7), and states the faster-convergence result against the conventional CTDE QMARL technique. The classical MARL baseline appears in the Fig. 7(b) legend and in the intro to that section, but the body text does not describe its result. Fig. 7(a) shows no significant difference with or without angle noise during meta-QNN angle training.
existing.value: The authors report, on the single-hop offloading environment, that in the local-QNN pole training the performance difference between angle noise present and absent is large, that the proposed scheme converges faster than the conventional CTDE QMARL technique, and that removing the pretraining causes a significant performance deterioration; in the meta-QNN angle training stage there was no significant difference with or without angle noise. The Concluding Remarks state that simulation results corroborated higher reward with faster convergence than a QMARL baseline and a classical MARL with the same number of parameters.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the number of environments is limited, angle training may incur overfitting, making the meta Q-network ill-posed, which motivates the angle-to-pole regularization.

assertions.certainty_reason: An unsupported motivation stated by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment in the paper measures overfitting or performance on an environment unseen in meta training.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since each locally trained QNN is represented by its two-parameter pole deviation, the pole memory can store K different QNN configurations using 2K parameters, regardless of the QNN size (the dimension of φ).
assertions.anchor: Introduction
quotes: Thanks to the two-parameter space of θ, the pole memory can store K different QNN conﬁgurations only using 2K parameters, regardless of the QNN sizes, i.e., φ dimensions.
assertions.certainty_reason: A design claim, stated without a count from the experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 1 lists the number of measurement parameters as 6, with the supplement stating two rotation gates per qubit for the measurement, so the 'two parameters' is per qubit; the stored pole for a whole QNN in the experiments holds more than two numbers. The claim also stores only the pole, so recovering a stored QNN needs the meta-trained angle parameters φ to be kept.

assertions.value: The authors state, as the rationale for few-shot learning in the pole domain, that a small QNN suffers from adapting to multiple environments, that scaling up the model is also challenging, that the measurement is an excellent kernel using very few parameters, and that the heritage of measurement enables fast catastrophic remembering to be more intuitive, reversible and memorable than the classical few-shot method.

Second, the measurement is an excellent kernel where the entangled quantum state is mapped to the observable
The last one is that the heritage of measurement enables fast catastrophic remembering to be more intuitive, reversible, and memorable than the classical few-shot method
assertions.certainty_reason: Reasoning offered by the authors, with citations for part of it, not tested against an alternative in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments never compare pole-domain few-shot training with fine-tuning the angle parameters or with a classical few-shot method.

assertions.value: The authors state that pole parameters are initialized to 0, so the measurement axes of all qubits start as the z-axes, and that in the meta-QNN angle training only one agent (the meta agent) is trained while it interacts with other agents that follow other policies.

assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own procedure.

assertions.value: The paper describes the pole memory procedure (Algorithm 2): the meta Q-network is trained over various environments, local QNN pole training fine-tunes it to a specific environment, and when a forgotten environment is met again during continual learning the pole parameters can be re-initialized from the pole memory.
assertions.anchor: Pole Memory for Fast Remembering Against Catastrophic Forgetting; Algorithm 2

Finally, when re-encountering a forgotten environment during continual learning, the pole parameters can be re-initialized as the meta Q-network in the pole memory.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own method.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence's wording ('re-initialized as the meta Q-network in the pole memory') and the Fig. 1 caption (which names an initial pole or the optimal pole of other environments) are not fully consistent about which pole is reloaded.

assertions.value: The authors state that, to cope with catastrophic forgetting, existing methods rely on replaying the entire previous experiences (Daniels et al. 2022), incurring a high computational cost.

assertions.value: The authors report, on the two-step game, that the initial tangent of the optimal Q-value distance is steep in Phase I when the pole memory is used, that in Phase II the comparison without pole memory cannot adapt to Env B while the proposed framework (α = 30◦ with pole memory) adapts, that utilizing a pole memory shows faster adaptation, and that Phase III shows faster adaptation similar to Phase I.
assertions.anchor: Effectiveness of Pole Memory in Fast Remembering (Fig. 6)
quotes: As shown in phase I of Fig. 6, the initial tangent of the optimal Q-value distance shows steep when the pole memory is utilized.
In phase II, the comparison (i.e., no pole memory) cannot adapt to Env B, while the proposed framework (denoted as α = 30◦ w. PM) adapts to Env B.
In addition, utilizing a pole memory shows faster adaptation. The result of phase III shows faster adaptation, which is similar to the results of phase I.

In summary, the pole memory enables QM2ARL to achieve faster adaptation, and the proposed framework (i.e., QM2ARL leveraging both angle-to-pole regularization and pole memory) shows faster and better adaptation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study on a toy game, read from a curve.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no numbers for the speed-up. The text reports all frameworks adapt better to Env A than Env B. The task is a three-state game with a reward flip in one state, and no comparison is made with replay or another continual-learning method.
